items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Brookmeyer and I got to be good friends

ctx.x: Any other ones that you feel are representative of – of course, then you have probably – how many charts do you think you have to your credit at this point?

I don‟t know. No idea. Any of our records with the later bands will give you an idea of what I do. I think the JVC CDs were better than the last two we did, because both of the last two were live, recorded live at concerts. It‟s good to get the spirit of a live concert, but the charts suffer a little bit. The band isn‟t always precise as you would like to have recorded forever, and tempos – you don‟t get a second chance at a tempo. You count out the wrong tempo, you‟re stuck with it. I want to also talk about…

weeks I got to play in the band, which was really a thrill for me. We played at Basin Street East. Then I came home, back to L.A. But those – the two musicians bars: Junior‟s and – what‟s the other one? I don‟t know. Can‟t remember – they were trouble. If you wanted to see somebody, you just go to one of those bars and everybody in town was there. So we spent too much time in there. But we survived. Gerry, when he was writing for Stan Kenton at that one little brief time, he wrote a chart called Youngblood, which…

items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: Brookmeyer has used synthesizers to really good effect on some of the things that he’s done in Europe.

ctx.x: In your own band, I’m not sure how to ask this question, has electronics entered into, even in the big band field. Actually what I think I’m getting at is does your rhythm section use electric instruments and if so does it change the sound?

No we don’t use them. We use an amp on the bass, but that’s — no, in the jazz world there hasn’t been a whole lot of that, in the straight ahead jazz, the mainstream. Brookmeyer has used synthesizers to really good effect on some of the things that he’s done in Europe. But mostly for a straight ahead jazz band, an electric sound doesn’t fit. It doesn’t have that grease that you like to say that humans have.
Any rock or popular music that’s come by your ears in the last 20 or so years that you really like?
